Mr. Printer ! i The usual public examination at the Danish and Lancasterian Schools was held on Monday last the 10th instant, the result of which appeared to give general satisfaction to all who were present. The orderly appearance of the children and their correct and precise answers to the questions put to them by the examiners, hear proof of the pains and attention bestowed on them, and does great credit to the principal teacher, the Reverend Mr. Tiiikmand, and the preceptors under him, by whom he is ably supported. The same praise must be bestowed on the female department of this institution, wherein besides the various branches taught the boys, is added useful and ornamental needle work, numerous specimens of which were exhibited at the examination, all done by the scholers. It is however to be regretted that þÿaltho Ilis Excellency the Governor General and several respectable Ladies and Gentlemen of this community were present, that many parents whose children are there instructed, were absent þÿ it is nevertheless to be hoped that the school will continue to prosper, and that its success may eventually preclude the necessity of sending their children abroad for education. As a Teacher in this School I believe 1 dare adventure to consider myself entitled to express my opinion, and 1 shall, in speaking separately of both notices, not omit endeavouring, according to my ability, to enlighten and correct public opinion. The author of the first notice in the paper of the 13th Sept, acknowledges his unqualified satisfaction as to the result of the examination of Sept. 10th, as well as in respect to the entire state of the establishment ; and lie awards the several teachers male and female much praise for the pains they have taken in the tuition of thechildren. cannot however perfectly agree with A þÿSubscriber in the hope he expresses þÿ that the þÿschool s s uccess may eventually preclude tiie necessity ol sending children abroad for þÿeducation. From the New Yoik Express. RAILROAD From ST. PETERSBURGH. TO MOSCOW. The Emperor of llussia admidst all the wars upon his hands, with Hungary, as the ally of Austria, and with Cireassla oh his own account, and with a personal superintendence of all the affairs of his extensive government, finds lime, we see, to look watchfully after the internal improvement of the empire. The railroad from St Peters burgh to Moscow, a distance of 420 miles, has been a favourite measure of his for ten years, and, during six of the time, the work was prosecuted under the direction of Col. George W. Whistler, of this country, as chief engineer. The work is, perhaps, the most stupendous of the kind in the country. It is very nearly straight; is 400 feet wide for the entire length; is laid with a double track, of a five feet guage, the rails being 67 pounds to the lineal yard ; is elevated from six to ten feet above the common level of the country, and in no place has grade exceeding '20 a feet to the mile The bridges have no spans exceeding two hundred feet, and are of wood built after the plan of Howe's improved " patent." so well known on the New England Roads, with a truss 24 feet in depth. An American house þÿ Messrs Harrison, Winans & Eastwick, of þÿBaltimore has the contract for the equipment of this road. þÿ They have already supplied it with 102 locomotive engines, averaging 25 tons weight J 72 passengers ears, 2.580 freight cats; two imperial saloon carriages, capable each of earrt ing the Imperial Court of Russia. All

this work has been done in Russia, and at an expense to the government of- nearly five millions of þÿdollars forty millions being the contemplated expense of the whole work. The Railroad Journal furnishes the following particulars of these equipments : " The Engines are of two classes, 62 are eight wheel engines for passenger travel, and iOO eight wheel engines for freight. The passenger engines are of one uniform pattern throughout, so that any portion of a machine will fit the same position on any other. They have each four driving wheels coupled six feet ir. diameter, and tiucks in front similar to the modern engines on the New England and New York roads Their general dimensions are as follows: Waste of boiler, 47 irx hos; length of lubes, 10 feet; number of lubes, 186 feet? diameter of tubes, 2 inches ; diameter of cylinders, 16 inches ; length stroke, of 22 inches. " The freight engines have the same capacity of boiler, the same number and length of tubes, with three pair of driving wheels, and a pair of small wheels in front. The driving wheels are only 4J feet in diameter, with 18 inch cylinders, and 22 inch stroke, all uniform throughout the workmanship and finish. " The passenger cats have the same uniformity. þÿ They are all fifty si feet in length by nine and a hall in width, and divided into three classes. The first class carrying 33 passengers, the second class 54 and the t hi i d class 8(1 passengers each. They are all provided with eight truck wheels each with
elliptic steel springs. The height cms are all of them thirty by nine and a half feel, made in uniform manner, having eight wheel ti ticks under each.
eighty feet in length ami nine and a half feet width, having double trucks and sixteen

AT18, i i mwi i i., r ' Wheels under each They are finished into five different compartments, the imperial mansion in the centre, 25 feet in length, fit ted up with every luxury for sitting or re dining, and With every eornlorl in every pan of it that the most ingenious mind can devise or the most refined tasie can desire, Spaci- , ous platforms are provided in the front and rear. The whole cost ot them exceed fifteen thousand dollars each. " The depots at each terminus, nhd the station houses and engine houses along the line, are on a plan uniform throughout, and on a scale equally imposing. " Fuel and water stations are placed at suitable points, engine houses are provided at the distance of 50 miles apart, built of the most substantial masonry oi circular form, 180 feet in diameter, surmounted with a dome, containing stalls for 22 engines each. Engines are to run from one engine house to another under only one heal, and are run back and forth from station to station, so that they are kept constantly in charge of the same þÿpersons. Repair shops are attached to every engine house, furnished with every tool or implement that thtf wants of the road can require. " Engine drivers have to go through the appropriate training bel'oie they are alio wed to take charge ot an engine, and every ar rangement provided thai skill, experience or ingenuity can demand. " The equipments have been built in Rus sia, in shops prepared by the contractors, and supplied by them with Russian labour The whole contract with Messrs. Harrison, Wi

nans dc Kastwiek, lias amounted to between four and five millions of dollars. They engaged to instruct a suitable number of Rus sian meehauics to take charge of engines when completed." Col. Whistler had the honor of prosecuting this noble woik nearly to its completion; and we remember well, when in Russia a few years since, to have witnessed the enei gv, the industry, and the enthusiasm which he brought to bear upon the woik Itis whole mind and strength were given to the work, and lie died just when he was about to realize the consummation of tiis labors, and lo fulfil the promise made lo the Einperor, ti.at in ten hours he would take him from his palace on the Neva and place him in ins Tartar palace within the walls of the Kremlin. This road was to have been completed during the present year ; and that the woik may not be long retarded hi consequence of thef death of Got. Whistler, the Empeior, through his Minister, M Bodisco, has ten dered the office of Superintendent to Major T. S. Brown, the able and efficient Chief Engineer of the New Eiie Railroad, and this appointment, we undersland, has Been conditionally accepted. It is equally gratifying and honorable, that our country men should thus be selected lo conduct the most siupcndoua woik of the kind in the old, Old World.

A Good Anecdote of a Mormon preacher is related by a correspondent of the N. O. Picayune, as follows : þÿ ' A few days since, at New Bedford one of the apostles sent forth to promulgate the faith of the Eattoi Hay Saints advertised that he would give an evening lecture, 'free gratis for nothing,' and earnestly called upon the " 1 he imperial saloon carriages are of good citizens to attend He procured a suitable room, had it well lighted, and when the time came found himself surrounded with

Somfe thirty or forty listeners. Aftet- a scree wiiat lengthy harrangue, in which he set forth the rise, progress and onward match or the true Normon church, lie finally finished , but just as the congregation were rising to depart, he Checked them for a moment with the remark that he hoped they would contribute enough to pay for the lighting of ilie room, which only amounted to the paltry sum of six dollars. A hat was carried round by an assistant apostle, and after circling round the room Was returned, with its contents of pics and pennies, to the follower of Joe Smith. Slowly he turned the hat over upon his desk, deliberately he counted the change þÿ two dollars and twenty five cents was the entire sum. The apostle looked about him. ' My hearers,' said he, with a small earthquake of smothered indignation in in his looks þÿ ' My hearets, the expenses of the room are six dollars þÿ the entire receipts are two dollars and twenty-five cents, and not the first red cent more I Now, I told you, in the first place, that my own services were gratuitous. 1 charge nothing for preach ing, but, I'll See this generation eternally d d before I'll find lights !'

African travellers have spoken of a tribe of negroes Who possess that ornamental appendage so much admirer! by Isjrd Monboddo þÿ a tail ; but their statements have never, I believe, received implicit credence. It appears, however, that a race of men with tails really does exist in the interior of Africa. In a recent sitting of the Academic des Sciences, M. du Comet related, that in 1842 lie found in the service of a friend at Mecca one of these wretches, the lowest assuredly ol mankind. The creature had an i xtarior prolongation of the vertebral column to the extent of three or four inciies. lie stated that lie belonged to the tribe of the Gliilaiies, whose territory is situated far beyond the Sennar, who are thirty or fort) 'thousand in number, worship the son, moon, the ser|«ent. and t'w sources of a great river (supjiosed to be the Nile.) to which last they immolate victims. They eat plains, roots, fruits, and raw flesh, and like it bleeding: are very partial to human flesh, and eat the bodies of their enemies, of all ages and both sexes, whom t.liey may slay in battle ! They, however, prefer the flesh of women and children as more succulent. They rarely exceed five feet :n height, are ill-proportioned, with long, thin bodies, long arms, longer and flatter hands and feet tiian the r. t of human kind, have the lower jaw large and long, the forehead narrow and excessively retreating, tie- cars long and deformed, the eyes small, black, brilliant, tiie

nose large and flat, tlie modtli large, the lips thick, the teeth strong and sharp, the hair woolly, but not abundant. The man examined by M. du Couret had b- en so long in slavery as to have forgotten his native language; but lie stated that, notwithstanding he had done all in his power to subdue the savage appetite, lie was twice a week seized with a rage for raw flesh, which his master satislied by giving him an enormous lump of mutton, and that if this were not done, lie felt that he could not refrain from slaying ami eating a woman or child. M. du Couret says, that the natural dispositions of this animal were good, that his fidelity to his master was striking, and that he was not without intelligence : but in the sJave-markets of the oast, where the race is not unknown, they are considered! everything that be detestable. þÿ Paris t airrospondeut oif ire Literary Gazette. þÿ YVii.i.mkr & thumbs Times. Affair of Jama i en, (From the Chronicle ) It will be within the recollection of our readers that in August 1848, the House of Assembly of the Island of Jamaica met in the full heal of the excitement naturally produced by the ruin with which the planting interests saw themselves threatened, and the widespread distress in which they were universally and to all appearance irrecoverably overwhelmed. The autumn session, as might he expected, was barren and infructuous; and on the 10th of December, a fortnight before the Christmas adjournment, tire House re solved " that it would not pass any bill raising a revenue beyond the ensuing 15th id February, until a measure of retrenchment consonant with the impoverished condition of the island be passed into law." The ordinary Revenue Acts, which would have expired with the closing year, were continued ; but their duration was limited to the 15th of February ; artd as the Legislative Council in Jamaica is not permitted to originate any bill, or to amend any money bill, the Governor had no choice but to take the Acts in this form or not at all. On the 23d of January the House met again, and on the 2d of February, thirteen days before the Revenue Acts would have expired, sent up to the Council a bill for reducing expenditure in certain departments of the public service þÿ By this bill, after a preamble reciting that the necessity for reducing the public expenditure was demonstrated by the disproportion between receipt and expenditure, it was enact-

ed that the salaries and allowances of the Governor, Judges, Clergy, and police officers of the island should, with some few exceptions, be reduced according to a graduated scale þÿ cutting ofi ten per cent from salaries utider 300/. and above 100/, and more than thirty per cent, ftom those of 2,000/. and upwards, the maximum limit of the scale þÿ This bill was rejected by the Council, which is principally composed of salaried officers. The Governor then prorogued the 1'arliamcnt for a few days, with the view of getting rid of the resolution above referred to ; and on re assembling on the 12th of Februaty, the I. owcr House consented to recede fiom its resolution, so far as to pass the two principal Revenue Bills, limited, however, in point of duration to the 1st of October, and fettered by appropriation clauses, which would have prevented any portion of the revenue to be raised under them from being available for paying the salaries of public officers or tfic stipends of the Clergy. In this state the Import Duties Bill and the Rum and Spirit Duties Bill were sent up to the Council; the first was passed under protest, and received the Governor's assent, the second was rejected, and two other hills sent up from the Assembly at the same time shared the same fate. The rupture was now complete. The Assembly memorialised the Home Government, praying for a change in the constitution of the Council þÿ the Council presented a counter memorial, defending itself from the attack, and denouncing in strong terms the

conduct of the Asscmbjy. Memorials fiorn the Judges and Cha rrnen of Quarter !Ses shoos followed, to which Lord Grey, of com so turned a deaf car. The Legislature was goon afterwards prorogued. On the 7th of July the Assembly pissed, by a majority of nineteen to eleven, a resolution declaring that, as her Majesty's Government hdd shewn no disposition to aflord tfie redress so urgently demanded, " the House considers that it will best consult the rights artd interests of their constituency by abstaining from any attempt at the further exercise of legislative functions until the people shall have expressed their decision on the course which the House has hitherto pursued." There are two sorts or vaiioiits of cochineal ; the best or domesticated, which the Spumaids called grunt, i Jino, or fine grain ; and the wild,

'1 lie cartridges in which these bullets are, have a layer of explosive mass next to the bullet, and the gt itpowder is at the bottom of the cartridge, which is put in at the lower end of the barrel. t)n the trigger being pulled a thin piece of steel (nailel) enters through- a hole irr the hack ol the barrel, and piercing the cartridge and the gunpowder, it proceeds to the explosive mass, which is similar to that which is employed for the usual peicussion þÿcaps. The promotion and improvement of the agriculture o( the colony and the encouragement of every branch of industry, constitute the objects of the Society. 2. Candidates for admission as members shall he proposed by two members at a general meeting and ballotted for at the succeeding, when a majority of votes will determine the election. 8. All members are to pay $ 2 quarterly in advance. Members allowing four quarterly bills to remain unpaid shall Cease to he members of the society, and their names shall he erased from the list. The anniversary meeting shall he held on the first Monday in the Month of October in every year, when the election of cilice bearers shall take place consisting of: 1 President, t Vice President, 1 Secretary and 1 Treasurer. 5. A general committee shall also he elected annually, consisting of the office hearers and twelve members. There shall besides be select standing committees for the ; more ready dispatch of business as shall be arranged from time to time at the general monthly meetings. 6. General meetings shall be held in the Governmenthcu.se on the first Monday of |

every second Month throughout the year. Special meetings may be convened at any time on a requisition to that effect signed by at least six members. Committee- meetings shill be held once a month, or oftener if j required. 7. The funds of the society to be held in deposit in the Hank of St. Thomas, to the j order of the Treasurer ; no bills shall be paid without the sanction of the President or Vice President, 8. Notice of motions shall be given on all questions relating to finance at a general meeting preceding that on which the subject i is disposed of, all such motions shall be recorded in the journals. 9. Motions on which previous notice has been given shall lake precedence of all others.
